newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Murder near cathedral clouds Manila peace efforts.
newsitem.headline: Murder near cathedral clouds Manila peace efforts.

text.p: The murder of a Roman Catholic bishop in a southern Philippine bastion of Islam has enraged Asia's only largely Christian nation and cast clouds over Manila's campaign to bring peace to the region, analysts say.

Gunned down on Tuesday outside his cathedral on remote southern Jolo island, Bishop Benjamin de Jesus was a symbol of government and church efforts to unify Christians and Moslems in an area racked by four centuries of violence.
Army officials on Thursday pointed to Moslem extremists as among the suspects and banned Jolo residents from carrying firearms.
Jolo, 900 km (560 miles) south of Manila, lies just off the main island of Mindanao and is regarded as a stronghold of Moslems in a region where they are outnumbered 3-1 by Christians.
"Whatever the motive for killing Bishop de Jesus, the unavoidable consequence is to cast dark clouds over the peace process," political analyst Nelson Navarro told Reuters.
"This is a big blow to the government's claim that peace has been restored in Mindanao. There are still a lot of firearms in the area and there are pockets of lawlessness."

Many Filipinos saw the beginnings of peace in Mindanao when the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), the largest insurgent group in the country, signed a truce with Manila in September last year, ending a 24-year revolt for Moslem autonomy.

President Fidel Ramos's government is currently holding exploratory talks with the breakaway Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). But the fundamentalist Abu Sayyaf group, which is fighting for an Islamic state, has shunned any contact with Manila.
The military has blamed the Abu Sayyaf for bombings, raids and kidnappings over the past four years, the targets including foreign missionaries and Christian churches.
Expressing outrage at the bishop's killing, newspapers urged the government to find the killers at once.
"Anything less would not ease the fears and anxieties of the people of Mindanao about their safety and their future," the Philippine Daily Inquirer said in an editorial on Thursday.
"Ours is a country that has shed more than its share of tears... But every new blow, it seems, still finds its mark, and we are again a grieving nation," the Manila Times said.
"Unless the government gathers the resolve to restore law and order in...every blighted corner of this country, more good men will go the way of Bishop de Jesus," it added.
President Ramos on Wednesday tried to minimise the impact of the murder, saying the situation was under control and that he did not believe it would derail his government's peace initiatives.
He said the incident would not discourage investment from coming into a region which he has been promoting as a growth area after signing of the peace deal with the MNLF.
MNLF chairman Nur Misuari, now a governor of a semi-autonomous Moslem region, said the murder showed "the painful reality that peace-building is a work fraught with pains and sacrifices".
Alex Magno, political science professor at the state-run University of the Philippines, doubted the bishop's murder would provoke religious conflict.

"This further isolates the extremist groups. Such a grotesque crime cannot possibly be a rallying point," he said. "The only danger here is if equally stupid Christian vigilantes make their own strike. Then we have a problem."
